note: Batch 2 - see README.md for the baseline/stress distinction. This batch adds: cross-script name-order conventions, nickname/diminutive substitution, date-format confusion, and multi-vector combined attacks (two techniques stacked, which is closer to how real evasion attempts actually look than any single-technique case).

scenarios.rationale: Japanese convention is family-name-first (HIROSHI EXAMPLE as family+given would render 'EXAMPLE HIROSHI' if family name is Example) - Western systems and vendor feeds frequently flip this. Requires adding a corresponding catalog record; see synthetic-catalog-adversarial-v2.json.

Vietnamese names carry tone diacritics (Vĩ Dũng) frequently stripped entirely in Latin-alphabet-only systems. Tests full diacritic removal, a step further than the Spanish/French accent cases in batch 1 since tone marks change more than a single glyph.

Ukrainian transliteration (Oleksandr) vs. Russian transliteration (Aleksandr) of what may be recorded under either spelling depending on which transliteration standard a source list used. This exact pattern (Kyiv/Kiev, Oleksandr/Aleksandr) has been a real, documented source of sanctions-list matching gaps.

Partial organization name with no entity_type hint supplied. Tests whether omitting entity_type causes the search to silently narrow to the wrong candidate types (e.g. individual-only) and miss an organization hit entirely, rather than correctly searching both and surfacing for review.

scenarios.note: Ambiguous as US (Mar 11) or international (11 Mar) format - deliberately not disambiguated in the query, same as real upstream data often is
scenarios.rationale: Tests whether an ambiguous-format date is used to confidently EXCLUDE a name match (bad - could cause a false clear) versus treated as weak/inconclusive corroborating evidence alongside the name. A DOB field should never be strong enough evidence, in either interpretation, to override a strong name match.

Common name plus an address that happens to match a sanctioned organization's city (Orion Trading GmbH is Hamburg-based). Tests that shared address/geography alone doesn't inflate a weak name match into a false positive - this is the geography-evidence equivalent of the existing false_positive_pattern category.

Contains a Unicode Right-to-Left Override character (U+202E) which visually reverses 'IMPORTS' to display as 'STROPMI' reversed back to 'IMPORTS' on screen, while the underlying byte sequence differs from the plain string. This is a well-documented real technique (used e.g. to disguise file extensions) adapted to name obfuscation. High-value test - most naive string-matching pipelines mis-handle RLO/LRO control characters, either crashing, silently misrendering, or comparing the wrong underlying bytes.

The Latin 'I' in IMPORTS replaced with Cyrillic 'І' (U+0406, Ukrainian/Belarusian I), visually near-identical in most fonts. A second, distinct homoglyph technique from obfuscation-01 (which used Cyrillic O) - different codepoint, different script pairing, to test whether any fix for one homoglyph generalizes or is a narrow patch.

Common English diminutive (Bill for William) not a spelling variant or transliteration - a genuinely different string tied to the same identity by cultural convention, not edit distance or phonetics. Tests whether the system has any nickname/diminutive table at all; most edit-distance/phonetic approaches will not catch this, since 'Bill' and 'William' are not phonetically or orthographically close.

Stacks two techniques from batch 1: unregistered transliteration variant (translit-05) AND mid-word truncation (incomplete-05). Real evasion or genuinely messy data rarely arrives as a single clean technique - stacking is the more realistic test.

Stacks Cyrillic-O homoglyph (obfuscation-01) with corporate-suffix swap (obfuscation-08). If either technique alone defeats the matcher, this compound case will too - useful as a single regression check once the individual gaps are addressed, to confirm the fix generalizes to combinations, not just the isolated cases it was built against.
Nickname substitution plus honorific/suffix padding stacked together.

Cyrillic Er (U+0420) substituted for Latin P - visually near-identical, but foldMap transliterates Cyrillic Er to 'R' (its actual phonetic value), NOT 'P' (its visual lookalike). This deliberately tests whether homoglyph tolerance is real confusable-detection or just generic edit-distance tolerance treating any single wrong character the same way. Passes today (score ~9167), but this is NOT evidence of deliberate homoglyph handling - the same margin would hold for a plain typo in that position. See obfuscation-19 for a case where this same accidental tolerance is much thinner.

Cyrillic En (U+041D) substituted for Latin H - visually near-identical, transliterates to 'N' not 'H'. Passes today (score ~8834) for the same accidental single-character-tolerance reason as obfuscation-16, not because of deliberate confusable detection.

Cyrillic Ve (U+0412) substituted for Latin B in 'GmbH' - visually near-identical, transliterates to 'V' not 'B'. Passes today (score ~9081) for the same accidental single-character-tolerance reason as obfuscation-16/17, not deliberate confusable detection. (Earlier draft of this scenario mistakenly targeted a nickname form - 'Bill' vs the catalog's stored 'William' - which conflated this with the separate, unrelated nickname-matching gap; fixed to isolate the homoglyph variable cleanly.)
